summary.title: How I Rewired My Brain to Become Fluent in Math
summary.one_liner: Fluency built through repetition, memorization and practice, rather than understanding alone, is what lets people master math and science, the author argues, drawing on her own path from math-phobe to engineering professor.
keywords: why students fail math despite understanding
takeaways: Understanding alone is fragile; it slips away without practice and repetition, and students often mistake understanding for competence.
Fluency builds understanding: repeated, varied practice creates 'chunks' that can be recalled quickly, especially under stress.
The author applies the same fluency-first approach she used to learn Russian to learning math and physics such as f = ma.
The article cites Japan's Kumon method and the Common Core standards as context for the debate over rote learning versus conceptual understanding.
summary.summary: A personal essay by an engineering professor describing how she went from failing school math to mastering calculus and engineering after leaving the Army at 26. She contrasts an understanding-centred teaching approach with the memorization and repetition used in Kumon and argues that procedural fluency underpins real understanding. She links this to chunking, drawing on Herbert Simon's chess research and studies of experts under stress, and to her own experience learning Russian. The piece is written as reflection and argument rather than a step-by-step tutorial.
